title: Paul's grief (Romans 9–10)
hookLine: Paul aches for his own Jewish people; how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news

lines: THE BEST NEWS, AND YOUR FAMILY.
THE MOOD DROPS LIKE A STONE.
cards: Someone gets life-changing news, runs home to share it, and finds their family sees it differently. Nobody stops loving anybody. It just aches.
Paul has just written that nothing can separate us from God's love. In the next sentence, the mood drops like a stone. He's thinking about his own family, his own people, the Jewish people.
Chapters nine through eleven are Paul wrestling, out loud, with grief and hope at once.

teach.b: Paul writes, in the King James Bible: "That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart." Continual. Not a passing sadness.
He'd almost give up his own place with Christ, he says, if it would help his kinsmen.

teach.h: THE ADOPTION, THE COVENANTS, THE PROMISES.
teach.b: Then he lists his people's honors: "Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises."
The patriarchs are theirs, and Jesus himself, Paul says, came from them. He calls them my brethren, my kinsmen, and speaks of his people with love.
His grief is that his own people, as a people, have not received Jesus as Messiah, and chapters nine and ten turn it over, painfully, without easy answers.

teach.h: NO DIFFERENCE: THE SAME LORD OVER ALL.
teach.b: Then in chapter ten he widens the door: there is no difference, he says, between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is rich to all who call on him. But how will anyone hear unless someone is sent?
He quotes Isaiah: "How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!"

teach.h: DUSTY FEET THAT BRING GOOD NEWS.
teach.b: Not faces, not voices: dusty feet that walked the long road to bring the news. Now something honest.
Over the centuries, some Christians used these chapters to look down on Jewish people, and that contempt fed real cruelty.

After the Holocaust, the Catholic Church, at the Second Vatican Council, firmly rejected that contempt and said the Jewish people remain dear to God, and a number of Protestant churches have said the same.
Churches still differ on how to understand Paul's hope today. But the chapters themselves open with an ache, not a sneer.

how: Some churches pray for the Jewish people in their regular intercessions, and the Catholic Good Friday liturgy includes a prayer for them; since the Holocaust, some churches read Romans 9–11 with particular care.

games.q: you're Paul. you've just written that nothing can separate us from God's love. your own people, as a people, see Jesus differently. what do you write next?
o: move on to practical advice for the church.
pour out your continual sorrow and love for them.
tell the Romans to leave them behind.
games.why: "I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart." three chapters of grief, love and hope for his kinsmen follow.

practice: Bring to mind Jewish people you know, a synagogue near you, or Jewish communities around the world, some facing real hatred today, and hold them with the love Paul had for his own.

If you pray, pray for their peace, their safety and their joy; if you don't, simply wish them well with each breath out. Then think of someone whose feet once brought good news to you, and give thanks for them.

wordCard.voice: Paul's grief. His continual sorrow for his own people, spoken with love, and the beautiful feet of those who carry good news.

orig.note: Greek: beautiful, lovely. some readers hear hōra, the season, in it: lovely because timely.

carryVoice: Your line: beautiful feet. Good news needs someone willing to carry it. See you tomorrow.
